topic.name: The Cartesian Equation of a Line

question.text:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

\[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty) \]
question.explanation:
Using the usual formula, we get

\[ \dfrac{x-(-1)}{0}=\dfrac{y-1}{2}=\dfrac{z-0}{-1} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty), \]

or equivalently

\[ \dfrac{x+1}{0}=\dfrac{y-1}{2}=-z, \]

which is problematic because $\dfrac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1+2t \\ -t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty) \]

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\dfrac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1,$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{y-1}{2}=-z, \; x=-1 \]

example.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero

question.text: Consider the straight line with the parametric equations \[ \begin{cases} x = -t \\ y = -3-2t \\ z = 4+7t \end{cases} \] for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
question.explanation:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -t \\ -3-2t \\ 4+7t \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -t \\ -2t \\ 7t \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, \end{align*} where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(0,-3,4)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle -1, -2, 7 \rangle.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

\[ \dfrac{x-0}{-1}=\dfrac{y-(-3)}{-2}=\dfrac{z-4}{7} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty). \]

Simplifying, we reach \[ \dfrac{x}{-1}=\dfrac{y+3}{-2}=\dfrac{z-4}{7}. \]

example.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form

question.text:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation \[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 4\\ 6\\ 9 \end{bmatrix} \]

for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
question.explanation:
We have the vector equation \[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 4\\ 6\\ 9 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty). \]

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(3,4,-5)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\left\langle 4, 6, 9\right \rangle.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

\[ \dfrac{x-3}{4}=\dfrac{y-4}{6}=\dfrac{z-(-5)}{9} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty). \]

Simplifying, we reach \[ \dfrac{x-3}{4}=\dfrac{y-4}{6}=\dfrac{z+5}{9}. \]

example.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form

question.text:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

\[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 5 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty) \]
question.explanation:
Using the usual formula, we get

\[ \dfrac{x - (-1)}{0}=\dfrac{y-2}{5}=\dfrac{z-4}{7} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty), \]

or equivalently

\[ \dfrac{x+1}{0}=\dfrac{y-2}{5}=\dfrac{z-4}{7}, \]

which is problematic because $\dfrac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2+5t \\ 4+7t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty) \]

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\dfrac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1$, as follows:

\[ \dfrac{y-2}{5}=\dfrac{z-4}7, \; x = -1 \]

example.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero

question.text: Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
question.explanation:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-1,2,5)$ and $Q(2,2,9).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ which is given by \begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle 2,2,9 \rangle - \langle -1,2,5 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 3,0,4 \rangle. \end{align*}

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by \[ \dfrac{x-(-1)}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-5}{4} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty), \] or equivalently \[ \dfrac{x+1}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-5}{4}. \]

But the above equation is problematic because $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2.$ For example, our two points $P\left(-1,2,5\right)$ and $Q\left(2,2,9\right)$ both have $y$-coordinates of $y=2.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{x+1}{3}=\dfrac{z-5}{4}, \: y =2 \]
